implementation_notes: SwiftUI's environment is the framework's context: ancestors publish values with .environment(\.key, value) or .environment(observableObject), descendants read them with the @Environment property wrapper, and the framework re-renders the readers when a value changes. Values provided as key paths have framework defaults, whereas reading an @Observable object by type requires that an ancestor actually published it - the documentation points out that reading a missing object throws and suggests the optional form when unsure. Overriding is per subtree, so a nested .environment(_:) shadows the outer value for everything below it.
pitfalls: Reading an object by type where no ancestor published it throws at runtime - use the optional form (@Environment(Library.self) private var library: Library?) when the environment may be empty.
@Environment is read-only: publishing requires a modifier applied higher in the hierarchy, so a view cannot provide a value to itself or its siblings.
Using the environment for screen state makes dependencies invisible and forces every preview and unit test to inject the value explicitly, which the framework does not check for you.

variants.name: TaskLocal values for structured concurrency
variants.implementation_notes: For non-UI code the equivalent is a task-local: declare @TaskLocal static var traceID, bind it with await $traceID.withValue(id) { ... } and read it anywhere inside that scope, including child tasks (async let, task groups and Task {} initializers inherit by copying). Detached tasks do not inherit, and outside a task the binding falls back to a thread-local for the scope, so synchronous helpers can read it too. Reading an unbound task local returns its declared default, which makes the default the fallback semantics of the provider.
pitfalls: Detached tasks do not inherit task-local values, so work started that way silently reads the default instead of the request's value.
The binding lasts exactly as long as the withValue closure; anything that escapes it (a stored closure, an unstructured task outliving it) sees the default again.
The binding is scope-bound by design, so there is nothing to reset on an error path - keep the read inside the withValue closure instead of copying the value out of it.
